extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political philosophy; scholars of early modern thought
extracted.subtask_short: reading Hobbes on honour and religion
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing the evaluative concepts Hobbes uses in Leviathan chapters on dignity, honour, manners, worthiness, and the natural origins and forms of religion. Focuses on what counts as honour/dishonour, public worth, human dispositions, and seeds/origins of religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: The publique worth of a man, which is the Value set on him by the Common-wealth, is that which men commonly call DIGNITY.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This value is expressed by offices of Command, Judicature, publike Employment; or by Names and Titles, introduced for distinction of such Value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honouring and Dishonouring (general definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: To Value a man at a high rate, is to Honour him; at a low rate, to Dishonour him. High and low are understood by comparison to the rate that each man setteth on himselfe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honour is the expression of opinion that someone has power to help or hurt; dishour is the opposite. The more difficult the aid, the more honour it shows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes/signs of Honour and Dishonour (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete acts or signs that constitute honour or dishonour: praying for aid, obeying, giving great gifts, promoting or flattering, yielding place or commodity, showing love or fear, praising, speaking with consideration, trusting, hearkening to counsel, imitating, honouring those another honours, employing in counsel, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each listed action is treated as a sign of valuing (honour) or undervaluing (dishonour). Opposites are explicitly indicated (e.g., obey = honour; disobey = dishonour; give great gifts = honour; give little gifts = dishonour). Also notes social/legal conventions: to do those things which the Law or Custome makes signs of Honour is to Honour; to refuse them is to Dishonour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign-created Honours
rubrics_metrics.description: A Soveraigne doth Honour a Subject, with whatsoever Title, or Office, or Employment, or Action, that he himselfe will have taken for a signe of his will to Honour him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sovereign power can institute whatever signs it pleases as marks of honour (example: Mordecay conducted in the King's garment). Such civil honours (magistracy, titles, coats) are signs of favour = power.

rubrics_metrics.name: What is Honourable (qualities and conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Honourable is whatsoever possession, action, or quality, is an argument and signe of Power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of honourable states or qualities: being honoured/loved/feared by many, lasting good fortune, riches, magnanimity, liberality, hope, courage, confidence, timely resolution, actions/speeches showing experience/science/discretion/wit, genuine gravity, conspicuousness for wealth/office/great actions, descent from conspicuous parents, equity joined with loss (magnanimity). Opposed are dishonourable: ill fortune, poverty, pusillanimity, parsimony, fear, irresolution, error/folly, false gravity, obscurity, obscure parentage, craft/shifting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles of Honour (function and origin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of Honour such as Duke, Count, Marquis, and Baron are Honourable as signifying the value set upon them by the Soveraigne Power of the Common-wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally titles of office/command (origins explained: duces, comites, marchiones, barones); over time these offices became mere titles to distinguish precedence and order, sometimes without possession or command.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worthinesse / Fitnesse (distinction from merit)
rubrics_metrics.description: WORTHINESSE is different from the worth, value, or merit of a man; it consists in a particular power, or ability for that whereof he is said to be worthy, usually named FITNESSE or Aptitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A man may be worthiest for an office by having the qualities required to discharge it well, yet may plead no right to it before another; merit presupposes a right (a thing due by promise), whereas worthinesse is about aptitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manners (broad definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: By MANNERS, Hobbes means not small decency of behaviour but those qualities of mankind that concern their living together in Peace, and Unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manners are the dispositions and qualities that enable social cohabitation and the pursuit of a continuing felicity (understood as continual progress of desire), not merely etiquette.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental human inclination: desire of power
rubrics_metrics.description: A perpetuall and restlesse desire of Power after power, that ceaseth onely in Death, is a general inclination of all mankind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This desire partly arises because present power cannot be assured without acquiring more; it explains why kings seek to secure power by laws or wars, and why desires shift (fame, ease, admiration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological/social causes of behaviours (taxonomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes lists multiple dispositions and their causal sources that incline men to particular social behaviours: competition produces contention; desire of ease and fear of death incline to civil obedience; love of arts and knowledge inclines to obedience; desire of praise inclines to laudable actions; receiving unrequitable benefits inclines to secret hatred; distrust of one's own wit inclines to preemptive striking in sedition; vain-glory inclines to ostentation or rashness; ambition arises from opinion of sufficiency; pusillanimity produces irresolution; frugality weakens collective endeavour; ignorance leads to credulity and adherence to custom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each disposition is tied to a specific cause and social consequence; Hobbes uses these to explain why men form commonwealths or fall into sedition and why social norms and religion arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural seeds of Religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Four Things, Naturall Seeds Of Religion: Opinion of Ghosts, Ignorance of second causes, Devotion towards what men fear, and Taking of things Casuall for Prognostiques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four are the natural sources from which varied religious ceremonies grow; differences in fancy, judgement, and passions produce diverse religions. Hobbes notes culture then shapes these seeds into organized religion for human or divine politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origins and form of natural religion
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion arises in Man from (1) desire of knowing causes, (2) consideration that things with a beginning must have a cause, and (3) observation of sequence/antecedence and consequence; combined these produce anxiety about the future and a belief in invisible agents (Gods/spirits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Men, lacking knowledge of second causes, invent invisible agents, conceive them as like human souls/ghosts, worship them as they would men (gifts, petitions, thanks, submission, premeditated words, swearing), attribute extraordinary events and prognosticate from casual occurrences. Some cultivate religion by human invention to secure obedience; others by divine direction.
